definition: Disgruntled means annoyed and dissatisfied, usually about a specific complaint or grievance.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word disgruntled. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know disgruntled should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The disgruntled diner sent back her cold pasta and asked, for the second time, to speak with the manager.
Miffed describes a small, passing flash of annoyance, while disgruntled suggests a deeper, grumbling dissatisfaction over a specific grievance.
Disgruntled stops well short of furious, which describes open, intense anger rather than testy dissatisfaction.

Annoyed is the all-purpose word for mild irritation at anything - a noise, a delay, a person. Disgruntled is more specific: sulkily dissatisfied over a particular grievance, usually a decision or arrangement that went against you. You can be annoyed for a second; disgruntled implies a grudge that lingers and grumbles.

Discontented describes a settled unhappiness with your overall circumstances - the job, the pay, the way things are. Disgruntled points at one concrete grievance and adds a grumbling, testy edge. A discontented worker wants a different life; a disgruntled one keeps stewing over the promotion that went to someone else.

Grumpy is a mood word: bad-tempered and complaining, often for no reason beyond a poor night's sleep. Disgruntled always has a reason - a specific grievance the person could name if asked. A grumpy neighbor snaps at everyone; a disgruntled neighbor is sore about the fence you built.

He muttered about the decision at his desk and started keeping a list of everything he had ever done for the company.
Marcus is not heartbroken or enraged; he is irritated and dissatisfied over one specific grievance, being passed over, which is exactly the grumbling, testy mood disgruntled describes.
Disgruntled almost always points to one concrete grievance: a fee, a delay, a decision that went against someone.

Unlike disaffected (loss of loyalty to an authority or institution) or disheartened (loss of hope or morale), disgruntled centers on irritation over one specific grievance, usually with a grumbling, testy tone.

When the building's management replaced the free laundry room with coin machines, the third floor took it hardest.
Petrov had washed towels there every Tuesday for eleven years without paying a cent.
She did not move out, and she did not stop doing laundry; she became, instead, thoroughly disgruntled.
Every trip downstairs came with a running commentary on the change, delivered to neighbors, to the doorman, and once to the machines themselves.
Asked if she was unhappy in the building generally, she looked offended.
The building was fine, she said.
It was the quarters she resented, and she could tell you exactly why.
